title: Biomimetic cells for studying T cell mechanotransduction - Nature Biotechnology
text:
Cell–cell interactions play fundamental physiological roles, especially in the immune system, but the cellular and mechanical features underlying these interactions remain difficult to study. Writing in Nature Methods, Yu et al. report the construction of artificial cells to study the mechanical forces operating in immunological synapses.Existing approaches to measure mechanotransduction in cell–cell contacts either rely on biochemical perturbations that offer limited control over cellular phenotypes or use synthetic materials that lack the dynamic complexity of living cells. The authors constructed artificial cells referred to as ‘key phenotype of interest cells’ (kpiCells). These cells consisted of a hyaluronic acid-containing biotinylated membrane, allowing subsequent functionalization with biotinylated compounds, and an inner endoplasm made of organic molecules. This dual architecture confers tunable stiffness and viscoelastic properties on kpiCells, which were shown by atomic force microscopy to span physiological ranges comparable to those of living cells.
